An armed revolt in Chiapas, in the far south of Mexico, launched on 1 January 1994, the day NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement, came into force. The rebels, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN), were mostly Indigenous Maya farmers. They seized San Cristóbal de las Casas and other towns, freed prisoners and burned land records.

The fighting lasted twelve days before a ceasefire. The rebels said free trade would ruin small maize farmers, and they demanded land, self rule and rights for Indigenous peoples. Their masked spokesman, Subcomandante Marcos, wrote statements that spread fast through the early internet, and 100,000 people marched in Mexico City against the army's crackdown.

Talks led to the San Andrés Accords on Indigenous rights in 1996, which the government never fully turned into law. The Zapatistas withdrew into self governing communities in the Chiapas highlands, which they still run. They took their name from Emiliano Zapata, hero of the Mexican Revolution, and they stand in a long line of resistance by the descendants of the Maya.
